narration: Part four. Your professor said you must be able to modify the code without AI. So here are three realistic requests, with worked answers. Each answer was tested in a scratch copy. The method is always the same. Find which files control the behaviour. Make the smallest change. Rebuild with the build command. Test in the guest. Then explain why it works. Keep a calm order: first say which function you will edit, then edit, then run. Do the exercises yourself first. Use the video only to check your answer.

Make the smallest possible change
`./scripts/xv6 build`, then `./scripts/xv6 run` and test
Explain why it works and what else it affects

narration: Request one: add a system call get prot that reports whether a page is writable. Return one if writable, zero if read-only, minus one if invalid. Start with the helper in vm dot c: reject addresses outside the process, walk the page table without allocating, require present and user, and return whether the writable bit is set. Then the wrapper in sysproc dot c fetches one argument and calls the helper. Then the wiring, exactly like m protect: a number, twenty-four, in syscall dot h, the extern and table entry in syscall dot c, a stub in usys dot S, the prototype in user dot h and the helper prototype in defs dot h. Test it by printing get prot before and after m protect: one, then zero.

narration: Request two: let len be a number of bytes, rounded up to whole pages. So m protect with five thousand bytes protects two pages. Only change protection in sysproc dot c changes. Reject zero and negative lengths first. Then convert: len minus one, divided by the page size, plus one. Why that form? Adding four thousand ninety-five before dividing could overflow for huge lengths. Subtracting first cannot. Then the same helper does the work. Mention the side effect: some vm test cases assume page counts, and would need updating. That shows you understand the consequences.

commentHints.comment: zero and negative lengths are still invalid

narration: Request three: when a process writes to a read-only page, print a clear message. The place is the default case in trap dot c, the user-space branch. Check that the trap is a page fault, and that the error code masked with seven equals seven: present, write, user. Print the process id, its name, and the faulting page, using P G R O U N D D O W N of the value that rcr two returns. Put the new print before the existing generic message. P G R O U N D D O W N is already available because trap dot c includes mmu dot h. Run vm demo and you will see both lines for each blocked write.

bits of err: 1 present, 2 write, 4 user

narration: Here are other likely requests, with the idea only. Think through each one on paper. Kill instead of returning an error: in sys read, if the destination is protected, set the killed flag, then return minus one. Refuse page zero: add a check for address zero to the first condition of the helper. Limit the number of pages: add a maximum to the count check. Return how many pages changed: count in pass two and return it instead of zero. Protect from the current address to the end of the heap: compute the page count from the process size. For each, say which file, which line, and what test you would run.

narration: Examiners love prediction questions. Here are four experiments, and their outcomes. Delete the lcr three line: the immediate-effect test fails. Merge the update into pass one: a rejected range leaves a program page read-only, and the test program gets killed. Remove the user-bit check from pass one: the stack guard page test fails, because the guard page is accepted. Change arg ptr w back to arg ptr in sys read: the kernel panics, a trap in kernel mode. Predict each result before you run it, then restore with git checkout.

bullets: Delete `lcr3(...)`: `mprotect takes effect immediately` fails
Merge the passes: a rejected range leaves a page read-only
Drop the `PTE_U` check: the guard-page checks fail
`argptrw` back to `argptr`: kernel `panic: trap`
Restore with `git checkout -- vm.c sysfile.c`

narration: Rapid fire. Answer each aloud before listening. Why must the address be page aligned? Because permissions apply to whole pages, so a mid-page address has no meaning. And length is in pages for the same reason. What does and-equals not W do? It clears only the write bit and leaves every other bit alone. Why two passes? So a failed call changes nothing. Why walk page directory with allocate zero? Validation must not create page tables, and a bad address must not allocate memory. What happens without the C R 3 reload? The processor may keep a cached writable translation, so a write could still succeed. Why V two P? C R 3 holds a physical address.

slides.description: Pause and answer before you listen
bullets: Why page-aligned address and length in pages?
What does `*pte &= ~PTE_W` do to other bits?
Why two passes? Why `alloc = 0`?
What if `lcr3` is missing?
Why `V2P(pgdir)` inside `lcr3`?

narration: Why does the child die but not the parent? The fault happens in the child's user mode, so the trap handler marks only that process killed. Decode trap fourteen error seven. Page fault; present, write, user. What would error six mean? A user write to a page that is not present. Why does fork keep protection? Copy u v m copies the flag bits into the child's new page. The two pages are independent copies. Is the stack guard page protectable? No. Its user bit is cleared by exec, so our validation rejects it. Can a process protect its own code at address zero? Yes, it is a user page. The project does not change null pointer behaviour.

slides.description: Pause and answer before you listen
bullets: Why does only the child die?
Decode `trap 14 err 7`; what would `err 6` mean?
Why does `fork()` keep protection? Shared or copied pages?
Why is the guard page rejected? Which bit?
Can a process protect its code at address 0?

narration: Why did read into a protected buffer panic the kernel? C R 0 W P makes kernel writes obey read-only pages, and a kernel-mode fault calls panic. How is it fixed? The output buffers of read, fstat and pipe are checked first, and the call returns minus one. Why is write from a protected buffer still allowed? The kernel only reads it. What happens to protected pages after exec, or after sbrk shrinks the heap? Exec builds a fresh address space. Shrinking frees the pages normally. New pages are writable. Is the check-then-write safe on a multi-processor kernel with threads? No, you would need locking or fault handling. On one processor with no threads, nothing can change the page between check and write. Why use a pipe in the tests? Because wait returns no exit status in x v 6.

bullets: Why did `read()` into a protected buffer panic the kernel?
How is it fixed? Why is `write()` still allowed?

Why does the test use a pipe instead of `wait()`?

narration: To close. The project in one sentence: a process can switch the write bit of its own pages off and on, safely, the hardware enforces it, and the kernel cannot crash or bypass it. Your remaining work: do the three exercises in docs slash viva dot m d without any assistant, answer the question bank aloud, and rehearse the demo on the machine you will present on. The deadline is the end semester exam plus three days. When you can rewrite set u v m write from memory and explain each line, you own it. Good luck.
